transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-07
Time: 15:00 UTC / 11:00 ET
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Kaur (Redwood SE), Evan Liu (CTO - Aperture), Priya Nair (Head of Security), Marcus Hale (SRE Lead), Leah Summers (QA Lead)

Auto-generated summary:
- Triage of recent pen test results, focus on high/critical items (auth, secrets, data leakage).
- Discussed patch cadence, SLA for remediation, integration with customer SDLC and Jira.
- Reviewed encryption/KMS options, HSM vs cloud KMS, data residency constraints (EU region requirement), and audit log retention.
- Agreed on next steps: share annotated findings, run targeted benchmarks, schedule follow-up triage next week.

Topics:
- Pen test findings (top 10, high/critical)
- Vulnerability management & patch cadence
- Secure SDLC and CI gating (SAST/DAST, PR gates)
- RBAC/SSO (SSO with Okta/SAML), session expiration policy
- Audit logs, retention, and export for compliance
- Encryption/KMS (customer-managed keys vs Redwood-managed, HSM options)
- Data residency and VPC/private deployment options

Action items (from transcript):
- Jordan to provide annotated spreadsheet and mapping to owners
- Samira to run KV cache and latency benchmark on sample dataset
- Marcus to create internal Jira tickets for each sev1-3 finding

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: Okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Today Samira and I will run through the pen test triage and the patch cadence alignment. Evan, Priya, you teamed up with Marcus and Leah, right?
00:12 Evan: Yep, thanks Jordan. Priya and Marcus are on this side, Leah as well. We've got the report from third-party pen test vendor — a fairly dense PDF with about 42 findings.
00:22 Priya: Morning all, quick note, a couple of the findings are false positives but there are 6 that we think are high or critical. We want to make sure triage is practical — our SLO is to close critical within two sprints.
00:34 Samira: Cool. Before we jump in, quick housekeeping — we'll try to call out the CVE or internal finding ID, severity, and suggested remediation. Apologies in advance, the auto-transcription sometimes munges product names — "Redwood dedicate" sometimes shows up, you might see that.
00:49 Marcus: Fine, yeah, we noticed some of the findings reference KV cache leakage, spelled like K-V cash in the doc — just to flag transcription weirdness.
00:59 Jordan: Great, okay first big one, Finding A-01: auth bypass pattern on admin API — severity: critical, CVSS 9.1. Externally reported exploit vector. In the pen test notes they used a stale JWT replay to access admin endpoints.
01:15 Evan: Right, that one is high priority for us. Our current token rotation is 24 hours, session TTL is 30 days, we probably need to shorten or rotate refresh tokens more aggressively.
01:27 Samira: On the Redwood side, we recommend enforcing short-lived access tokens and rolling refresh tokens with detection of replay — we can enable session revocation hooks. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS that can revoke keys — that helps but doesn't replace token rotation.
01:45 Priya: How does that work with our Okta SSO? We use SAML assertions and Okta issues a token to our app. If Redwood rotates tokens more frequently, will it break SSO flows?
01:56 Samira: Good question. We can coordinate so Redwood issues short-lived tokens post-auth exchange. The SAML assertion lifecycle is independent; we can map assertions to short-lived internal tokens and drop long-lived session cookies. There might be some integration work with your IdP.
02:12 Leah: Small ask — when you say short-lived, what are we talking? Seconds, minutes? Our UX folks worry about too-frequent reauth.
02:20 Samira: Typically 15 minutes access tokens with 24-hour refresh rotating per use is a common pattern. But we can do sliding windows and incremental refresh to avoid UX churn.
02:32 Evan: Okay that sounds doable. Next finding, A-07: secrets in logs — devs found AWS keys in application logs. Sev: high.
02:41 Priya: Ouch. That was from a staging run where an env var got printed. We're patching the log statements but want to know if Redwood keeps any transient logs on hosted API or in Dedicated pools.
02:52 Jordan: For hosted, Redwood stores request and response metadata for observability, but we strip credentials and redaction rules by default. For Dedicated we can disable request logging or configure retention. We also have a redact-at-ingest pipeline but we should look at your exact patterns.
03:12 Marcus: Is that pipeline configurable for custom regex? Our secrets detector uses a custom pattern.
03:19 Samira: Yes, we support custom redaction rules — regex-based or token lists. For Private deployments we can run that pipeline in your VPC so logs never leave your network unless you opt-in.
03:31 Evan: Good. On data residency — we have to ensure EU customer data stays in eu-west-1. Are there any telemetry or analytics that might leak region?
03:40 Jordan: We have a region-scoped routing policy; requests routed to eu-west-1 stay in-region. For multi-region failover we have an opt-in fallback; we'll disable that for your account to ensure strict residency. We'll also provide an audit log showing region of processing for each request.
03:58 Priya: Audit logs — retention and format. We need immutable logs for 12 months and a CSV export for compliance.
04:06 Samira: We can export audit logs to your S3 or your SIEM via secure delivery. Retention configurable up to several years; immutable retention requires customer-side write-once policies, but we can provide append-only logs and cryptographic signing if needed.
04:21 Evan: Nice. Next big area: encryption and KMS. The pen test flagged potential exposure if key rotation is slow. We use AWS KMS; we want to understand Redwood support for CMKs vs Redwood-managed keys.
04:34 Jordan: Redwoods supports both: Redwood-managed keys by default; customer-managed keys (CMKs) via cross-account access or bring-your-own-key. For highest assurance we support HSM-backed keys through cloud KMS or on-prem HSM in Private deployments. We have an integration guide which Samira will share.
04:48 Priya: Are key operations logged? We need to see key usage events in audit logs.
04:53 Samira: Yes, key ops are logged: encrypt/decrypt/sign requests, and we can forward CloudTrail-like events to your SIEM. For dedicated/private we can integrate with your KMS endpoint and mirror logs.
05:04 Marcus: One of the medium findings references an outdated dependency that surfaces a CVE — CVE-2024-3389 (example). Is that something Redwood can patch in our hosted stack or are we responsible?
05:15 Jordan: For hosted API, Redwood manages runtime dependencies; we push security patches. For Dedicated, patching policy can be coordinated — we can apply critical patches during maintenance windows. For Private you run the stack, we provide guidance and patches you can apply.
05:31 Evan: So for Dedicated we need to align maintenance windows. Our ops team wants a weekly patch window, not more than 2 hours downtime. Can Redwood do rolling updates?
05:41 Samira: Yes, our Dedicated pools support rolling deploys with zero-downtime for stateless endpoints; KV cache migrations may require short warm-up. We can set up canary rollouts and automatic rollback on errors.
05:52 Leah: For SDLC — what about gating in CI? We want SAST/DAST integration and pre-deploy checks to prevent regressions.
06:00 Samira: We have a security checklist and CI integration hooks; for example we provide a test harness for S2I that runs sample prompts and checks for known regressions. We also recommend adding a pre-deploy eval suite that blocks PRs on quality/security regressions.
06:15 Priya: How do you handle vulnerability severity classification? The pen test vendor used their own scale — can we map to CVSS and Redwood's triage?
06:23 Jordan: We'll map vendor severities to CVSS and to our internal triage — critical (9.0+), high (7.0-8.9), medium, low. We'll annotate the spreadsheet with both mappings and suggested SLAs.
06:35 Evan: About SSO and RBAC — we use Okta and want per-team roles with least privilege. Can Redwood sync Okta groups to roles?
06:44 Samira: Yes, SAML/SCIM sync is supported — sync groups into RBAC roles and automate provisioning. We also offer fine-grained route-level permissions for admin APIs. There's an audit trail for role changes.
06:57 Marcus: Do session tokens created via SCIM have admin privileges? Concerned about over-privilege.
07:03 Samira: No, SCIM is for provisioning accounts and group membership. RBAC enforces what actions a user can take. We'll help set up role templates: admin, security_viewer, dev_ops, app_user.
07:15 Priya: Another finding (A-19) — improper error handling leaking stack traces in responses from model endpoints. Sev: medium. The pen tester reproduced it by sending malformed input.
07:26 Samira: That's usually a runtime-level exception leak. We can add a middleware to sanitize error responses and also add fuzzing to your CI to catch regressions.
07:35 Leah: Great — we can add a test case. I'll take that back to QA.
07:39 Evan: On patch cadence, Priya mentioned two sprints for criticals. Can Redwood support that SLA for hosted endpoints?
07:48 Jordan: For hosted, critical security patches are prioritized and we push hotfixes within 72 hours typically, depending on complexity. For Dedicated, we can commit to customer windows and more strict SLAs via a contract. For Private, depends on your release process.
08:02 Priya: Need to clarify definitions: what counts as critical vs high for SLA.
08:07 Jordan: We'll include a definitions appendix in the spreadsheet and map each finding.
08:12 Evan: Ok, shifting to logging/export — we need to ensure logs include request id, user id, region, and key usage when applicable.
08:22 Samira: We'll add those fields in the audit log schema. We'll provide a sample CSV and SIEM mapping.
08:29 Marcus: Any PII handling concerns? Some prompts include customer names. We need redaction at ingest and also allow us to opt out of storing full prompts.
08:38 Samira: Yes, we support prompt-level redaction and retention policies. You can set a do-not-store flag on certain routes — we honor it. For regulatory workloads, Private deploy with local storage is recommended.
08:50 Priya: Have there been any incidents historically where keys were exfiltrated? We need incident history for the security review.
08:58 Jordan: We can share a sanitized incident history as part of our security pack — high-level summaries, root cause, and mitigations. I'll attach that to the follow-up.
09:07 Evan: About benchmarks — Samira, you mentioned running KV cache tests. Can you emulate our typical 30k token document retrieval patterns?
09:16 Samira: We can approximate if you share a representative sample set. We will run two load patterns: bursty queries and long context sequences, measure p99 latency, token throughput, and memory use. We'll also look for left-over cache keys after session expiry.
09:29 Marcus: On the pen test's 'token leakage' finding, the vendor observed prefix inference from logs stored in a shared cache. Is there a per-customer cache namespace option?
09:38 Samira: Yes, cache namespaces are scoped per-tenant. Shared caches are only for older multi-tenant config; we'll confirm your environment uses isolated namespaces, but we can enforce namespace policies for Dedicated/Private.
09:50 Leah: A small transcription glitch in the vendor notes called it 'K-V cash' — not sure if that confused the triage earlier, ha.
09:56 Jordan: (laughs) we've seen "K-V cash" and "Redwood dedicate" before.
10:03 Evan: Anything about legal/procurement? We need a doc showing the SLA and indemnities related to security patches.
10:11 Jordan: We have a standard security addendum, and for Dedicated we can negotiate tougher SLA clauses. I'll loop in legal if needed after we map the critical findings.
10:21 Priya: For the remediation timeline, we prefer a plan that includes immediate mitigation (WAF rules, ingress filters), short-term patch in the next deploy, and a permanent fix in the next minor release.
10:32 Samira: Sounds good. We can propose mitigations per finding: blocklist WAF, rate-limit suspicious endpoints, and code fix. We'll annotate the spreadsheet accordingly.
10:42 Evan: Ok let's call out three highest-priority items that need on-call paging if exploited.
10:48 Priya: A-01 (auth bypass), A-03 (privilege escalation via admin UI), A-07 (secrets in logs) — those three.
10:59 Jordan: Noted. We'll mark them as Sev-1 for the triage call and propose immediate mitigations.
11:05 Marcus: Quick ask — do you support per-tenant key rotation schedules? We want monthly rotation for some keys and quarterly for others.
11:12 Samira: Yes, per-key rotation policy supported for CMKs. For Redwood-managed keys, rotation cadence can be configured per-customer.
11:21 Leah: For our QA checklist, can Redwood provide a sample test harness and example prompts to include in our CI?
11:27 Samira: Absolutely — I'll drop a GitHub repo with examples and a small runner that exercises the main endpoints and checks for regressions and error sanitization.
11:35 Evan: Great. Anything else?
11:38 Jordan: Quick recap: Jordan will share annotated spreadsheet and security pack; Samira will run KV-cache/latency benchmarks; Marcus will open JIRAs and Priya will confirm SDLC/policy windows. We'll meet on 2026-09-14 for triage.
11:54 Evan: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
11:58 Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials. Bye.

End of transcript.
